subject: Quantitative Aptitude
description: Sample space, dice/coins, cards, conditional probability, complementary events

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled once. The probability of getting a number greater than 4 is:
questions.explanation: Sample space S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, n(S) = 6. Favourable outcomes (>4) = {5, 6}, n(E) = 2. Probability = 2/6 = 1/3. Read 'greater than 4' carefully — it does NOT include 4 itself. If it were 'at least 4', the favourable set would be {4, 5, 6} → 3/6 = 1/2.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: Two fair coins are tossed simultaneously. The probability of getting at least one head is:
questions.explanation: Sample space = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, |S| = 4. 'At least one head' = complement of 'no head' (= TT). P(no head) = 1/4. P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. Direct count: HH, HT, TH all qualify → 3/4 ✓. The complementary trick (1 − P(none)) is invaluable for 'at least one' problems.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: From a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards, a card is drawn at random. The probability of drawing a King OR a Heart is:
questions.explanation: Inclusion-Exclusion: P(K ∪ H) = P(K) + P(H) − P(K ∩ H). 4 Kings, 13 Hearts, 1 King-of-Hearts (counted in both). So 4 + 13 − 1 = 16 favourable cards. P = 16/52 = 4/13. Trap option 17/52 forgets to subtract the overlap (the King-of-Hearts).
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled. The probability that the sum of the numbers showing is 8 is:
questions.explanation: Sample space = 6 × 6 = 36 ordered outcomes. Outcomes giving sum 8 — list them: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) → 5 outcomes. Probability = 5/36. Note: (4,4) is one outcome (not two, because two dice are independent and we're listing ordered pairs but the same pair). Common counts to memorise — sums 7 (=6/36, the most likely), 6 = 5/36, 8 = 5/36, 5 = 4/36, 9 = 4/36, 2 or 12 = 1/36 each.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: A bag contains 5 white and 4 red balls. Two balls are drawn one after another WITHOUT replacement. The probability that BOTH are red is:
questions.explanation: Without replacement → conditional probability. P(1st red) = 4/9. After taking one red, 3 reds remain among 8 total. P(2nd red | 1st red) = 3/8. Joint probability = (4/9) × (3/8) = 12/72 = 1/6. With replacement, it would be (4/9)² = 16/81. Use the multiplication rule for sequential events; conditioning is the key word for 'without replacement'.

questions.stem: If P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3 and A, B are independent events, then P(A ∩ B) is:
questions.explanation: Independent events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12. Don't confuse with mutually exclusive events: P(A ∩ B) = 0 (cannot occur together; addition rule gives P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)). Always note the relationship — independent ≠ mutually exclusive — exam papers test this distinction.

questions.stem: From 7 boys and 4 girls, a committee of 3 is to be formed. The probability that the committee has exactly 2 girls is:
questions.explanation: Total ways to pick 3 from 11: ¹¹C₃ = 165. Favourable = (pick 2 girls) × (pick 1 boy) = ⁴C₂ × ⁷C₁ = 6 × 7 = 42. Probability = 42/165 = 14/55. Verify by simplifying — divide by 3: 42/165 = 14/55 ≈ 0.2545. Check sum across all girl-counts: P(0G) + P(1G) + P(2G) + P(3G) = 35/165 + 84/165 + 42/165 + 4/165 = 165/165 = 1 ✓.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: A box contains 3 defective and 12 non-defective light bulbs. One bulb is picked at random. What is the probability that the selected bulb is NOT defective?

options.option_text: 1/5, the probability of picking a defective bulb
4/5, the probability of picking a non-defective bulb
2/5, misread as two out of five possible outcomes
3/5, using defective count as the numerator over 5

questions.explanation: Total bulbs = 3 + 12 = 15. Non-defective = 12. P(not defective) = 12/15 = 4/5. Option A (1/5 = 3/15) is the probability of a defective bulb — a classic complement confusion where candidates compute the complementary event instead of the required one.

questions.stem: The letters of the word EXAMINATION are written on 11 separate cards, one letter per card, and one card is drawn at random. What is the probability that the drawn card shows a vowel?

options.option_text: 4/11, counting only the 4 distinct vowel types used
5/11, from missing one repeated vowel in the count
6/11, all six vowel occurrences counted correctly
7/11, from mistakenly including a consonant as vowel

questions.explanation: EXAMINATION: E, X, A, M, I, N, A, T, I, O, N — 11 cards total. Vowels by position: E(1), A(3), I(5), A(7), I(9), O(10) = 6 occurrences. P = 6/11. Option A (4/11) is wrong because it counts only the 4 distinct vowel letters (E, A, I, O) and ignores that A and I each appear twice on separate cards.

questions.stem: In a class of 40 students, 25 play cricket, 20 play football, and 10 play both. A student is chosen at random. Given that the selected student plays cricket, what is the probability that the student also plays football?

options.option_text: 1/4, dividing the overlap count directly by class size
2/5, using conditional formula P(F∩C) divided by P(C)
1/2, dividing the common count by football players only
3/8, based on those who play only cricket but not both

questions.explanation: P(F|C) = P(F∩C)/P(C) = (10/40)÷(25/40) = 10/25 = 2/5. Option A (1/4 = 10/40) ignores the conditioning and uses the full class as the sample space. Option C (1/2 = 10/20) incorrectly conditions on football instead of cricket — it answers the reverse conditional.

questions.stem: A number is chosen at random from the integers 1 to 30. What is the probability that the number is divisible by at least one of 3 or 5?

options.option_text: 8/15, adding multiples of 3 and 5 without removing overlap
1/3, by counting only the multiples of 3 in the range
7/15, by inclusion-exclusion: (10 + 6 − 2) divided by 30
1/2, an overestimate from double-counting shared multiples

questions.explanation: Multiples of 3 in 1–30: 10 numbers. Multiples of 5: 6 numbers. Multiples of 15 (both): 2 numbers (15 and 30). By inclusion-exclusion: 10 + 6 − 2 = 14 favourable. P = 14/30 = 7/15. Option A (8/15 = 16/30) is the classic error of adding 10 and 6 directly without subtracting the overlap of 2.

questions.stem: A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one at a time WITH replacement after each draw. What is the probability that the two balls drawn are of different colours?

options.option_text: 13/25, the probability both balls are the same colour
24/25, obtained by doubling the individual colour products
2/5, taking just the product of one-way colour fractions
12/25, accounting for both orderings of the two colours

questions.explanation: P(different) = P(Red then Blue) + P(Blue then Red) = (4/10)(6/10) + (6/10)(4/10) = 24/100 + 24/100 = 48/100 = 12/25. Option A (13/25) is P(same colour) = (4/10)²+(6/10)² = 52/100 — it answers the complementary event. Option C (2/5) forgets to account for both orderings.

questions.stem: In a factory, machine P produces 60% of the total output and machine Q produces the remaining 40%. Machine P generates 3% defective items and machine Q generates 5% defective items. A defective item is picked at random. What is the probability that it was produced by machine Q?

options.option_text: 9/19, the posterior probability attributable to machine P
10/19, derived by applying Bayes' theorem to defect data
2/5, the prior production share of machine Q in the plant
5/8, from comparing only the two machines' defect rates

questions.explanation: P(defective ∩ P) = 0.6×0.03 = 0.018; P(defective ∩ Q) = 0.4×0.05 = 0.020; total P(defective) = 0.038. By Bayes': P(Q|defective) = 0.020/0.038 = 20/38 = 10/19. Option A (9/19 = 18/38) is P(P|defective) — the reversed posterior. Option D (5/8) ignores production weights and divides defect rates 5/(3+5) directly.

questions.stem: Five job-offer letters meant for five different candidates are randomly inserted into five pre-addressed envelopes, one letter per envelope. What is the probability that no letter reaches its intended recipient?

options.option_text: 3/8, the probability exactly one letter lands correctly
4/5, from each letter having a 4 out of 5 mismatch chance
11/30, derived from the derangement count D(5) over 5!
1/2, a common intuitive answer when no formula is applied

questions.explanation: Number of derangements D(5) = 5!(1 − 1/1! + 1/2! − 1/3! + 1/4! − 1/5!) = 120×(44/120) = 44. Total arrangements = 5! = 120. P = 44/120 = 11/30. Option B (4/5) is a naive per-letter argument that ignores dependencies between placements. Option A (3/8 = 45/120) is P(exactly one correct placement), not zero — a different and harder-to-spot error.
